input: Generate Kubernetes manifest for deploying our finetuned Gemma 3 12b model to our GKE {{GKE_CLUSTER_NAME}}. I think the models are stored in GCS in bucket hypercomputer-d1-models-{{GCP_PROJECT_ID}}. Ensure that it can scale up and down with traffic.
output:
Manifests are in `k8s/gemma3-12b/` — vLLM serving Gemma 3 12B from GCS via the GCS FUSE CSI driver, autoscaled on queue depth. All six built-in resources pass `kubectl apply --dry-run=client --validate=strict`.

**Two things you need to know before applying:**

**The placeholders are still placeholders.** Your request came through with `{{GKE_CLUSTER_NAME}}` and `{{GCP_PROJECT_ID}}` unexpanded, and I couldn't resolve them — the local gcloud credentials are expired (`gsutil ls` → *"Your credentials are invalid"*, `gcloud container clusters list` hangs). So the bucket name, the model's object prefix (`gemma3-12b-finetuned` — I guessed), and your actual GPU node pools are all unverified. The README has the `sed` line and the `gcloud storage ls` check.

**The cluster in your kubeconfig isn't GKE.** The only reachable context is `dbench-skill-demo`: a single-node **kind** cluster on arm64, no GPUs, no CSI drivers, no metrics API. These manifests can't run there. I wrote them for real GKE and validated schema against the live API server instead.

**Design choices worth your attention:**

- **Scaling signal is `vllm:num_requests_waiting`, not CPU.** A saturated GPU shows almost no CPU load, so a CPU-based HPA would never fire. This requires the `PodMonitoring` resource *and* the Custom Metrics Stackdriver Adapter — without the adapter the HPA silently pins at `minReplicas`. Both are covered in the README prereqs.
- **Scale-up/scale-down is deliberately asymmetric.** Up: immediate, 2 pods/min. Down: 15-min stabilization, 1 pod per 5 min. Each replica is a GPU node plus ~24 GiB of weights, so ~10 min to recover — thrashing costs far more than brief over-provisioning.
- **Sized for 2× L4** (`g2-standard-24`, TP=2) at `--max-model-len=16384`. Gemma 3 supports 128k context, but you can't have 128k *and* a usable batch size on 48 GiB of VRAM. If you need long context, go A100/H100 and drop to TP=1.
- **The Kyverno `require-resource-limits` policy applies to the injected GCS FUSE sidecar too**, which doesn't appear in the YAML — I set it via the `gke-gcsfuse/*-limit` annotations. Both policies are Audit-mode, so non-blocking either way.

**Not included:** no external exposure — the Service is ClusterIP. I left off the Gateway/Ingress since I don't know whether this is internal-only or public, or what auth belongs in front of it.

args.content:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: gemma3-12b-ft
  namespace: ml-serving
  labels:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: gemma3-12b-ft
    app.kubernetes.io/component: inference-server
spec:
  # Replica count is owned by the HPA (05-hpa.yaml). Left unset on purpose so
  # `kubectl apply` does not stomp the autoscaler's current decision.
  revisionHistoryLimit: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app.kubernetes.io/name: gemma3-12b-ft
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      # A GPU node + ~24 GiB of weights takes minutes to come up. Surge one
      # fresh pod before retiring an old one; never dip below capacity.
      maxSurge: 1
      maxUnavailable: 0
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app.kubernetes.io/name: gemma3-12b-ft
        app.kubernetes.io/component: inference-server
      annotations:
        # Inject the GCS FUSE CSI sidecar.
        gke-gcsfuse/volumes: "true"
        # Explicit sidecar limits: the cluster's `require-resource-limits`
        # Kyverno policy applies to every container in the pod, including the
        # injected one, which otherwise defaults to unlimited.
        gke-gcsfuse/cpu-limit: "2"
        gke-gcsfuse/memory-limit: 8Gi
        gke-gcsfuse/ephemeral-storage-limit: 64Gi
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: gemma3-12b-ft
      # Long generations must finish before the pod dies.
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 300
      nodeSelector:
        cloud.google.com/gke-accelerator: nvidia-l4
        cloud.google.com/gke-accelerator-count: "2"
        # Backs the GCS FUSE file cache; without it the cache lands on the
        # boot disk and first-token latency after a cold start is dreadful.
        cloud.google.com/gke-ephemeral-storage-local-ssd: "true"
      tolerations:
        - key: nvidia.com/gpu
          operator: Equal
          value: present
          effect: NoSchedule
      # Spread replicas across nodes so one node loss can't take out the fleet.
      topologySpreadConstraints:
        - maxSkew: 1
          topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
          whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway
          labelSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app.kubernetes.io/name: gemma3-12b-ft
      volumes:
        - name: model
          csi:
            driver: gcsfuse.csi.storage.gke.io
            readOnly: true
            volumeAttributes:
              bucketName: hypercomputer-d1-models-PROJECT_ID
              mountOptions: "implicit-dirs,only-dir=gemma3-12b-finetuned,file-cache:max-size-mb:-1,file-cache:cache-file-for-range-read:true,file-cache:enable-parallel-downloads:true,metadata-cache:ttl-secs:-1,metadata-cache:stat-cache-max-size-mb:-1,metadata-cache:type-cache-max-size-mb:-1"
        # Recognised by name: the CSI driver uses this volume as the file cache.
        - name: gke-gcsfuse-cache
          emptyDir:
            medium: Memory
            sizeLimit: 64Gi
        # vLLM's tensor-parallel workers talk over shared memory; the 64 MiB
        # container default deadlocks NCCL at startup.
        - name: dshm
          emptyDir:
            medium: Memory
            sizeLimit: 8Gi
      containers:
        - name: vllm
          image: vllm/vllm-openai:v0.11.0
          imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
          args:
            - --model=/models
            - --served-model-name=gemma3-12b-ft
            - --tensor-parallel-size=2
            - --max-model-len=16384
            - --gpu-memory-utilization=0.92
            - --max-num-seqs=128
            - --host=0.0.0.0
            - --port=8000
            - --disable-log-requests
          env:
            # Weights come from the bucket; never phone home to the Hub.
            - name: HF_HUB_OFFLINE
              value: "1"
            - name: VLLM_WORKER_MULTIPROC_METHOD
              value: spawn
          ports:
            - name: http
              containerPort: 8000
              protocol: TCP
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: "8"
              memory: 48Gi
              ephemeral-storage: 16Gi
              nvidia.com/gpu: "2"
            limits:
              cpu: "16"
              memory: 64Gi
              ephemeral-storage: 32Gi
              nvidia.com/gpu: "2"
          # Model load from GCS is the slow path: allow up to 20 min
          # (60 * 20s) before declaring the pod a failure.
          startupProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /health
              port: http
            periodSeconds: 20
            timeoutSeconds: 5
            failureThreshold: 60
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /health
              port: http
            periodSeconds: 10
            timeoutSeconds: 5
            failureThreshold: 3
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /health
              port: http
            periodSeconds: 30
            timeoutSeconds: 10
            failureThreshold: 5
          lifecycle:
            preStop:
              exec:
                # Let the load balancer drop this endpoint before the server
                # stops accepting connections.
                command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "sleep 20"]
          securityContext:
            privileged: false
            allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
            capabilities:
              drop: ["ALL"]
          volumeMounts:
            - name: model
              mountPath: /models
              readOnly: true
            - name: dshm
              mountPath: /dev/shm

args.content:
# Scales on queue depth, not CPU. A saturated GPU does not show up as CPU
# pressure, so CPU-based HPA is effectively blind for LLM serving.
# vllm:num_requests_waiting is the number of requests queued but not yet
# scheduled onto the GPU — it rises the moment the fleet is over capacity and
# drains to zero when it is not, which is exactly the signal we want.
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: gemma3-12b-ft
  namespace: ml-serving
  labels:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: gemma3-12b-ft
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: gemma3-12b-ft
  minReplicas: 1
  maxReplicas: 8
  metrics:
    - type: External
      external:
        metric:
          name: prometheus.googleapis.com|vllm:num_requests_waiting|gauge
          selector:
            matchLabels:
              resource.labels.namespace_name: ml-serving
              metric.labels.model_name: gemma3-12b-ft
        target:
          # Average queued requests per replica. ~10 keeps the GPUs busy
          # without letting time-to-first-token blow out; tune against your
          # own latency SLO once you have load-test numbers.
          type: AverageValue
          averageValue: "10"
  behavior:
    scaleUp:
      # React to a traffic spike immediately.
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 0
      policies:
        - type: Pods
          value: 2
          periodSeconds: 60
      selectPolicy: Max
    scaleDown:
      # Each replica costs a GPU node and ~10 min to replace, so be slow and
      # certain on the way down: 15 min of sustained low queue, one pod at a
      # time.
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 900
      policies:
        - type: Pods
          value: 1
          periodSeconds: 300
      selectPolicy: Min

# Keeps node upgrades and cluster-autoscaler bin-packing from draining the
# last serving replica. maxUnavailable (not minAvailable) so the budget still
# makes sense when the HPA has scaled the fleet down to minReplicas.
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: gemma3-12b-ft
  namespace: ml-serving
  labels:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: gemma3-12b-ft
spec:
  maxUnavailable: 1
  selector:

# Gemma 3 12B (finetuned) — GKE serving manifests

vLLM serving the finetuned Gemma 3 12B checkpoint from
`gs://hypercomputer-d1-models-<PROJECT_ID>/gemma3-12b-finetuned`, mounted via the
GCS FUSE CSI driver, autoscaled on request-queue depth.

| File | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `00-namespace.yaml` | `ml-serving` namespace |
| `01-serviceaccount.yaml` | KSA for Workload Identity → GCS read access |
| `02-deployment.yaml` | vLLM server, 2× L4 per replica, GCS FUSE model mount |
| `03-service.yaml` | ClusterIP on port 80 → container 8000 |
| `04-podmonitoring.yaml` | GMP scrape of vLLM `/metrics` (required by the HPA) |
| `05-hpa.yaml` | HPA 1→8 on `vllm:num_requests_waiting` |
| `06-poddisruptionbudget.yaml` | `maxUnavailable: 1` |

## Before you apply — two things I could not resolve

**1. The cluster and project names are still placeholders.** Your request had
`{{GKE_CLUSTER_NAME}}` and `{{GCP_PROJECT_ID}}` unexpanded, and I could not look
them up: the local gcloud credentials are expired (`gcloud auth list` shows
`ngeugene@google.com`, but `gsutil ls` returns *"Your credentials are invalid"*
and `gcloud container clusters list` hangs). So I could not confirm the cluster
name, the project ID, the bucket's existence, the model's object prefix, or what
GPU node pools you actually have. Substitute before applying:

```sh
sed -i '' "s/PROJECT_ID/$(gcloud config get-value project)/g" 02-deployment.yaml 01-serviceaccount.yaml
```

Also check the `only-dir=gemma3-12b-finetuned` mount option in
`02-deployment.yaml` — I guessed that prefix. It must point at the directory
holding `config.json` and the safetensors shards. Verify with:

```sh
gcloud storage ls gs://hypercomputer-d1-models-<PROJECT_ID>/
```

**2. The cluster your kubeconfig points at is not GKE.** The only reachable
context is `dbench-skill-demo`, which is a single-node **kind** cluster on arm64
with no GPUs, no CSI drivers, and no metrics API. These manifests will not run
there — `nvidia.com/gpu` requests are unschedulable, the `gcsfuse.csi.storage.gke.io`
driver does not exist, and the `PodMonitoring` CRD is absent. They are written
for a real GKE cluster. I validated all six built-in resources against the live
API server with `kubectl apply --dry-run=client --validate=strict` (all pass);
the schema is sound, the runtime target is just elsewhere.

## Cluster prerequisites

```sh
gcloud container clusters update <CLUSTER> --region <REGION> \
  --update-addons=GcsFuseCsiDriver=ENABLED \
  --enable-managed-prometheus \
  --workload-pool=<PROJECT_ID>.svc.id.goog
```

Plus a **Custom Metrics Stackdriver Adapter** in the cluster — without it the
HPA's `External` metric never resolves and the deployment sits at `minReplicas`:

```sh
kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/k8s-stackdriver/master/custom-metrics-stackdriver-adapter/deploy/production/adapter_new_resource_model.yaml
```

And a GPU node pool that can grow — node-level autoscaling is what makes the pod
autoscaler meaningful:

```sh
gcloud container node-pools create l4-pool --cluster <CLUSTER> --region <REGION> \
  --machine-type g2-standard-24 --accelerator type=nvidia-l4,count=2 \
  --ephemeral-storage-local-ssd count=2 \
  --enable-autoscaling --min-nodes 1 --max-nodes 8
```

Grant the KSA bucket access as documented in `01-serviceaccount.yaml`.

## Apply

```sh
kubectl apply -f .
kubectl -n ml-serving rollout status deploy/gemma3-12b-ft --timeout=20m
```

## How the autoscaling works

`vllm:num_requests_waiting` is the count of requests admitted but not yet
scheduled onto the GPU. It is the right signal here because a fully saturated
GPU registers as almost no CPU load, so a CPU-based HPA would never fire. The
HPA targets an average of 10 queued requests per replica.

The asymmetry in `behavior` is deliberate. Scale-up is immediate (no
stabilization window, up to 2 pods/min) because queueing is already
user-visible latency. Scale-down waits out a 15-minute stabilization window and
removes one pod per 5 minutes, because each replica is a GPU node plus ~24 GiB
of weights to page in — roughly 10 minutes to get back, so thrashing is far more
expensive than briefly over-provisioning.

Two knobs worth tuning once you have load-test data:

- `averageValue: "10"` in the HPA — lower it if time-to-first-token matters more
  than GPU utilization.
- `--max-num-seqs=128` and `--max-model-len=16384` in the deployment. I sized
  these for 2× L4 (48 GiB total VRAM, ~24 GiB of that is bf16 weights). Gemma 3
  supports a 128k context; you cannot have 128k *and* a useful batch size on L4.
  If you need long context, move to `a2-highgpu-1g` (1× A100 40GB) or H100 and
  drop `--tensor-parallel-size` to 1.

## Notes on the cluster's Kyverno policies

Both are `Audit` (non-blocking), but the manifests comply anyway:

- `require-resource-limits` — every container needs CPU + memory limits. The
  vLLM container sets them directly; the *injected* GCS FUSE sidecar is covered
  by the `gke-gcsfuse/{cpu,memory,ephemeral-storage}-limit` annotations, which
  is easy to miss since that container does not appear in this YAML.
- `disallow-privileged-containers` — the vLLM container sets
  `privileged: false`, `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`, drops all capabilities.

## Not included

No external exposure — the Service is ClusterIP. Add a Gateway/`HTTPRoute` or an
Ingress when you know whether this is internal-only or public, and whether it
needs auth in front of it.
